title: Bara Brith
subtitle: Welsh tea bread with spiced fruit
excerpt: Bara brith is a Welsh fruit bread where dried fruit is soaked overnight in strong tea before being stirred into a simple batter. The result is a dense, moist loaf with a dark, treacle crumb. Serves 10 to 12 slices.
sourceNotes: Bara brith translates from Welsh as 'speckled bread', referring to the visible pieces of dried fruit in the crumb. Welsh recipe collections from the 19th century onwards include versions made both as a yeasted enriched bread and as a quick-bread batter (the eggless version). S. Minwel Tibbott, Welsh Fare: A Selection of Traditional Recipes (1976, National Museum of Wales), gives both the traditional yeasted form and the quick-bread version that became the standard in most Welsh homes from the mid-20th century. The tea-soaking method is characteristic: no fat is added to the batter; the tea-soaked fruit provides all the moisture.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze. Thaw slices individually at room temperature or toast from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The fruit must be soaked overnight in tea. The loaf improves after a day in a tin.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dried fruit soaked overnight in strong black tea absorbs the liquid, plumping the fruit and lending the loaf its dark colour and moist crumb. No added fat is needed in the batter.

content.text: Bara brith starts the evening before. The dried fruit goes into a bowl with strong black

and soaks overnight. By morning the fruit is plump and the tea has taken on colour and sweetness from the fruit. The soaking liquid becomes part of the batter, which is why the loaf is moist and dark without any added fat.

The loaf takes about an hour in the oven at a low temperature. It is done when a skewer comes out clean and the crust has darkened. It improves with a day's rest; cut too soon, the crumb can be gummy. Eat in thick slices with salted butter, or toasted.

items.prepNote: strong, hot, made from 2 tea bags

content.text: The evening before baking, put {{mixed-dried-fruit}} of mixed dried fruit and {{dark-brown-sugar}} of dark brown sugar into a large bowl. Pour over {{black-tea}} of hot strong tea. Stir, cover, and leave overnight at room temperature.
Heat the oven to 160°C fan (180°C conventional). Grease and line a 900 g loaf tin with baking parchment.

Stir the beaten egg (and marmalade, if using) into the soaked fruit. Sift in {{plain-flour}} of plain flour, {{baking-powder}} of baking powder, and {{mixed-spice}} of mixed spice. Fold gently until just combined.

Pour into the prepared tin and level the surface. Bake for 55 to 65 minutes until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. If the top browns too fast, cover loosely with foil for the last 15 minutes.
Leave to cool in the tin for 20 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Leave for a day before slicing if possible. Serve in thick slices with salted butter.

items.symptom: Loaf is dense and gummy in the centre
items.cause: Underbaked, or cut too soon after baking
items.fix: Test with a skewer that must come out clean. Cool completely before slicing, ideally wait a day.

items.symptom: Loaf has a dry, crumbly crumb
items.cause: Fruit not soaked long enough, or too much flour
items.fix: Overnight soaking is necessary. The fruit should have absorbed most of the tea. Check the flour measurement.

items.symptom: Top cracks and darkens while the centre is still raw
items.fix: Lower to 150°C fan and extend the baking time. Cover with foil if the top darkens.

content.text: Bara brith is as Welsh as cawl or Welsh rarebit. It appears at every bake sale, chapel tea, and family kitchen table in Wales. The name simply describes what you see: a dark, speckled bread. Traditionally it was made with yeast, the fruit added to a bread dough and the whole thing left to rise before baking. The quick-bread version, which needs no proving time, became standard as domestic baking habits changed in the 20th century. Both are correct; the tea-and-fruit character is what makes it bara brith, not the leavening method.
